It was Gargi's fourth visit to the Aizawl branch that month, and Lalremsiami, at the counter, recognised the account number on the transfer slip before she looked up.
"Same beneficiary?" she asked.
Gargi nodded, cheeks pink. "His business account is frozen. It's just until Friday."
Lalremsiami didn't scold. She lowered her voice. "Can I ask a few things, just between us? Have you met him in person?"
"Not yet. He's in Malta."
"Has he ever video called?"
"His camera..." Gargi trailed off.
Lalremsiami had seen this story in the bank's fraud training: the same charming engineer, the same frozen account, scripts shared by organised groups who do this all day. Gargi wasn't foolish. Gargi was up against professionals.
"Would you sit with our fraud officer for ten minutes before sending? No pressure. I'll come too."
Gargi looked at the slip for a long moment, then nodded.

Urmila looked. The man was handsome, the light perfect. "That's the fifth good-deed photo this month."

Arohi's smile faded. "Some. For his daughter's school fees. And the hospital."

Arohi set the phone face down. "What do I even do?"

I'm Alka, and I've known Nazia since school. Over three months, I watched something that scared me.
Every few weeks she asked to borrow a little money. Then I saw her at the bank, sending money abroad. She told me it was for Daniel, an engineer on an oil rig she'd met online. His salary was stuck. His daughter was sick. His equipment was held at customs.
She'd never met him.
I wanted to shout, "Are you mad?" I didn't. I'd read that scolding just makes people defend the scammer harder.
So over coffee I asked questions. "Has he ever video called? Has he ever sent you anything? Why does every problem need money?" She got quiet. Then she said, "He always has a reason."
I showed her an article about scam centres that work in shifts, with scripts. Professionals. She read it twice.
She didn't stop that day. But she agreed to come with me to the cyber cell on Saturday.

qa.q: Who did Nazia say she was sending money to?
qa.a: To Daniel, an engineer on an oil rig she'd met online.

qa.q: What was Alka feeling as she watched Nazia send money?
qa.a: Alka felt scared and frustrated, wanting to shout but choosing to stay gentle.

qa.q: Why did Alka ask questions instead of scolding?
qa.a: Alka knew scolding could make Nazia defend the scammer harder, so gentle questions and an article about professional scam centres helped Nazia think.

qa.q: How did Nazia react to Alka's questions?
qa.a: Nazia went quiet and admitted he always has a reason, and agreed to go to the cyber cell on Saturday.

Bank teller's note, Friday. Written by Urmila, counter 3.
Avni, a regular customer, came in today for her fourth international transfer this month. Each time, a larger amount, to a different name. Today she seemed anxious and was checking her phone constantly.
I didn't refuse or lecture. I asked, gently, "Is this for family?" She said it was for her fiancé, a doctor working abroad, whom she hasn't met yet. He needs help with a legal fee.
I asked, "Has he ever asked you to keep this secret?" She hesitated, then nodded.
I explained, as kindly as I could, that we see this often, that these are organised groups who build a persona over months, and that she is not foolish for believing it. I showed her our bank's scam warning leaflet.
With her agreement, we paused the transfer and I called our fraud team, who spoke to her in the back office. She left with the cyber police helpline number written on her hand.

qa.a: Today was her fourth international transfer this month.

qa.a: Urmila was probably concerned and careful, seeing a worrying pattern but wanting to avoid shaming Avni.

qa.q: What did Urmila do instead of refusing or lecturing?
qa.a: Urmila asked gentle questions, explained that organised groups build personas, showed the scam leaflet, paused the transfer with Avni's agreement and called the fraud team.

qa.q: How did Avni seem to feel at the counter?
qa.a: Avni seemed anxious and hesitant, checking her phone and admitting she'd been asked to keep it secret.

Tuesday night
Wasim sent money again today. That's the fifth time since March.
Her name is Sophia. She's "a UN nurse in Syria." They talk every night. He showed me her photos: beautiful, always in scrubs, never in a video. Every week there's a new problem. Her pay is delayed. She needs a travel permit. Her phone was confiscated.
I wanted to yell, "Wasim, wake up." But I remember how my uncle reacted when my cousin was scammed: shouting, and my cousin only went deeper.
So tonight, over chai, I just asked, "Has she ever video called?" "Has any money ever come back?" "Why does every problem have a price?" He got defensive. Then quiet.
I read online that these scams are run like companies, with teams, scripts and targets. Wasim isn't stupid. He's up against a whole business.
Tomorrow I'll show him the article and offer to go with him to the cyber cell. No yelling.
Uday

qa.a: "A UN nurse in Syria."

qa.a: Uday feels worried and frustrated, wanting to yell but choosing patience to avoid pushing Wasim deeper.
